dx: Acute Q fever pneumonia (Coxiella burnetii) in a sheep farmer after lambing season
case: A 39-year-old woman who raises sheep comes to the physician because of fever, severe headache, muscle aches, and a dry cough for 6 days. Three weeks ago she helped deliver lambs and handled placentas without gloves. Her temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows crackles over the left lower lung field and no rash. Leukocyte count is 7,600/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000), platelet count is 112,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), AST is 96 U/L (10 to 40), and ALT is 118 U/L (10 to 40). Chest x-ray shows patchy opacities in the left lower lobe. Serum antibodies to phase II antigens of Coxiella burnetii rise fourfold between acute and convalescent samples. The diagnosis is acute Q fever pneumonia.

questions.stem: Two weeks later, her neighbor, a schoolteacher who lives 2 km (1.2 miles) downwind of the farm and has never handled animals, develops the same illness. Which of the following best explains how both women acquired the infection?
options: Bites from ticks carried off the pasture in the wool of infected sheep
Inhalation of wind-borne dust contaminated by birth products of the sheep
Ingestion of well water contaminated by the urine of infected farm livestock
Inhalation of spores released while processing wool and hides from the farm
approach: Link the exposure (lambing, placentas) and the phase II antibody rise to Coxiella burnetii.
Recall that Coxiella is shed in huge numbers in placentas and birth fluids of sheep, goats, and cattle, and is acquired by inhaling contaminated aerosols or dust.
A neighbor with no animal contact fits wind-borne spread of a hardy organism, which rules out routes that need direct contact.
questions.why: Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular gram-negative bacterium carried by farm animals. Infected ewes shed very large numbers of organisms in the placenta and birth fluids at lambing. The bacterium forms a small, tough cell form that resists drying, heat, and disinfectants, so it survives for months in dust and can travel kilometers on the wind. Inhaling only a few organisms can cause infection, which is why outbreaks reach people who never touch animals. Unlike the Rickettsia species, it does not need an arthropod vector to infect humans, and it usually causes no rash.
whyNot: Ticks can carry Coxiella among animals, but tick bites are a rare route for humans and cannot explain a neighbor 2 km away with no animal contact. Tick bites are the classic route for tularemia and Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
Water contaminated by animal urine is the classic source of leptospirosis, which enters through skin abrasions or mucous membranes, not airborne spread to a neighbor.
Spores from wool and hides cause inhalational anthrax (woolsorter's disease), which presents with hemorrhagic mediastinitis and a widened mediastinum, and the neighbor never handled wool.

questions.stem: The contaminated dust particles she inhaled were about 1 µm in diameter. Which of the following host defenses is the first to meet these organisms at the site where her infection began?
options: Trapping in bronchial mucus with upward clearance by ciliated cells
Filtration by nasal hairs and impaction on the nasal turbinates
Neutralization by secretory IgA on the bronchial mucosal surface
Uptake by alveolar macrophages aided by surfactant opsonins
approach: Relate particle size to where particles deposit: large particles stop in the nose and large airways, and particles of about 1 to 2 µm reach the alveoli.
Her pneumonia is in the alveoli, so the first defense there is the one present in the alveolar space.
Alveoli have no cilia or mucus, so the alveolar macrophage, helped by surfactant proteins A and D, is the first line of defense.
questions.why: Particles larger than about 10 µm are filtered in the nose, particles of about 2 to 10 µm land on the mucus of the conducting airways and are carried up by cilia, and particles under about 2 µm reach the alveoli. The alveolar surface has no ciliated cells or mucus. Resident alveolar macrophages ingest particles there, and surfactant proteins A and D bind microbes and act as opsonins to speed this uptake. Coxiella survives inside the acidic phagolysosome of the macrophage, so clearing it requires T cells that release interferon-gamma to activate the macrophages.
whyNot: The mucociliary escalator clears particles of about 2 to 10 µm that land in the bronchi and bronchioles. It ends before the alveoli, where 1 µm particles deposit.
Nasal filtration removes large particles, more than about 10 µm, and does not stop 1 µm particles.
Secretory IgA works on mucosal surfaces of the upper and conducting airways, and she has no prior specific IgA to this organism. Alveolar fluid relies mainly on macrophages and IgG.

topics: Particle size and deposition in the airway

questions.stem: While she has a fever, her skeletal muscle capillary blood has a higher PCO2 and H+ concentration than when she is well. The normal P50 of adult hemoglobin is about 27 mm Hg. Compared with when she is well, which of the following best describes her hemoglobin in these capillaries?
options: Higher P50 and lower O2 saturation at a PO2 of 40 mm Hg
Higher P50 and higher O2 saturation at a PO2 of 40 mm Hg
Lower P50 and lower O2 saturation at a PO2 of 40 mm Hg
Lower P50 and higher O2 saturation at a PO2 of 40 mm Hg
approach: Higher PCO2, higher H+, and higher temperature all lower hemoglobin's affinity for O2 (the Bohr effect plus the effect of heat).
Lower affinity shifts the dissociation curve to the right, so a higher PO2 is needed for 50% saturation, which means a higher P50.
At any given tissue PO2, a right-shifted curve gives a lower saturation, so more O2 has been released to the tissue.
questions.why: H+ binds histidine residues and CO2 binds the amino ends of the globin chains, and both stabilize the deoxy (T) form of hemoglobin. Heat also lowers O2 affinity. The curve moves right, P50 rises, and at a tissue PO2 of 40 mm Hg less O2 stays bound, so more is unloaded to working, febrile tissue. In the lungs the reverse happens through the Haldane effect: as hemoglobin binds O2, it releases H+ and carbamino CO2, which helps CO2 leave the blood.
whyNot: A higher P50 means lower affinity, so saturation at the same PO2 must fall, not rise. This pairing is internally inconsistent.
A lower P50 means higher affinity, which would raise saturation at a given PO2. This pairing is also inconsistent.
A lower P50 with higher saturation is a left shift, seen with low PCO2, alkalosis, hypothermia, low 2,3-BPG, carbon monoxide, or fetal hemoglobin, the opposite of her state.

topics: Shifts of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve

questions.stem: Her opacities involve alveoli and the surrounding airways about 0.5 mm in diameter. Which of the following mainly keeps airways of this size open during normal breathing?
options: Irregular hyaline cartilage plates within the airway wall
C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings bridged by smooth muscle
Outward pull by attached elastic alveolar walls
A thick layer of submucosal glands stiffening the wall
approach: An airway about 0.5 mm wide is a bronchiole, since bronchioles are under about 1 mm in diameter.
Bronchioles have no cartilage and no submucosal glands, and goblet cells give way to club cells as they get smaller.
With no cartilage, bronchioles stay open because the elastic alveolar walls attached around them pull outward (radial traction).
questions.why: Bronchi have cartilage plates, submucosal glands, and goblet cells. Bronchioles lose the cartilage and glands, their goblet cells thin out and give way to club cells, and they have a relatively thick smooth muscle layer. Their walls are tethered to the surrounding alveolar septa, and the elastic recoil of those septa pulls the bronchioles open, more so as lung volume rises. This is why loss of alveolar walls, as in emphysema, lets bronchioles collapse during expiration.
whyNot: Irregular cartilage plates support bronchi, which are larger than about 1 mm. They disappear at the bronchiole level.
C-shaped cartilage rings with the trachealis muscle bridging them are found in the trachea, not in small airways.
Submucosal glands are found in the trachea and bronchi and are absent from bronchioles. Glands secrete mucus and do not hold an airway open.

topics: Radial traction and small airway patency
